conventions.convention: Minkowski coordinates are unscaled: each chosen complex embedding contributes its real and imaginary parts, without √2.

Full Euclidean lattices have n ≥ 1 and an integer basis that is also a real basis; covolume is the absolute basis determinant. Adapted successive-minima vectors are a real basis, not necessarily an integer basis of the whole lattice.
The fundamental parallelotope uses 0 < t_i ≤ 1. Strict Minkowski permits measurable origin-symmetric convex sets; the non-strict volume inequality requires compactness.
Successive minima dilate the compact, convex, origin-symmetric body with nonempty interior while holding the lattice fixed; λ₀ = 0 and 0 < λ₁ ≤ ⋯ ≤ λₙ < ∞.
The geometry-of-numbers measure route assumes AC explicitly and discharges Countable Choice through AC; the discrete-subgroup lemma itself permits dimension and rank zero without Choice.
The ideal-lattice covolume theorem and absolute ideal norm definition apply to nonzero integral ideals.
Logarithmic coordinates are log|σx| at real places and 2 log|τx| at complex places, with real coordinates first; unit logarithms lie in the literal coordinate-sum-zero hyperplane.
The regulator is an absolute deleted-row determinant of a fundamental-unit logarithmic matrix; the empty determinant is 1 at rank zero.
S is a finite set of nonzero prime ideals, containing only finite places; the S-unit rank is r₁ + r₂ − 1 + |S|.
Cyclotomic conductors are least admissible embedding indices for full cyclotomic fields. Reduced indices are odd or divisible by 4; φ(1) = ord₁(ℓ) = 1.
Frobenius is arithmetic, inducing the residue-field power map and sending ζ_f to ζ_f^ℓ when ℓ does not divide f.
Quadratic Gauss sums require an odd prime and a chosen primitive root; their square and generated quadratic field are independent of that choice, but the sum changes by a Legendre sign.

load_bearing.statement: Assume AC. For n ≥ 1, a full lattice Λ and a compact, convex, origin-symmetric C ⊆ Rⁿ, vol(C) ≥ 2ⁿ covol(Λ) implies that C contains a nonzero lattice point.
For a number field K and a nonzero integral ideal a, the unscaled Minkowski lattice has covolume 2^(−r₂)√|d_K| · N(a).
Assume AC. Every class in Cl(O_K) contains an integral ideal b with N(b) ≤ (4/π)^r₂(n!/nⁿ)√|d_K|.
Let K be a number field and B ≥ 1 be real. Only finitely many nonzero integral ideals a ⊆ O_K satisfy N(a) ≤ B.
For every integer n ≥ 1 and real R ≥ 1, only finitely many monic integer polynomials of degree at most n have all complex roots, counted with multiplicity, of modulus at most R.

For a subgroup Γ of a finite-dimensional real vector space with norm topology, discreteness, finite intersection with every bounded set, and generation by an R-linearly independent finite tuple as a free abelian group are equivalent.
Assume AC. The discrete subgroup λ(O_K×) spans H = {x : Σx_i = 0} over R and is a full lattice there of rank r₁ + r₂ − 1.
Assume AC. O_K× ≅ μ(K) × Z^(r₁+r₂−1); the unit group is finitely generated of that rank and has torsion subgroup μ(K).

Assume AC and the stated compact symmetric convex-body, full-lattice and adapted-basis hypotheses. The centroid deformation Φ is Borel and odd, has image volume (∏λ_i)vol(C), has no collisions modulo 2Λ, and Φ(int C) ∩ Λ = {0}.
Assume AC. For n ≥ 2, B ≥ 1 and a degree-n number field with |d_K| ≤ B, there is an integral primitive element whose every conjugate has modulus at most √(B+2).
For a prime p and a ≥ 1, O_Q(ζ_pᵃ) = Z[ζ_pᵃ], (p) = (1−ζ_pᵃ)^φ(pᵃ), and the power-basis discriminant has absolute value p^[p^(a−1)(a(p−1)−1)].
If [KL:Q] = [K:Q][L:Q] and gcd(d_K,d_L) = 1, products of integral bases give an integral basis of O_KL = O_K O_L, and d_KL = d_K^[L:Q] d_L^[K:Q].

If O_K = Z[α] and the monic minimal polynomial reduces modulo p as ∏g_i^a_i, then pO_K = ∏(p,g̃_i(α))^a_i, with distinct primes of residue degrees deg g_i, independently of integer lifts and without AC.
For reduced f ≥ 1 and f = ℓᵃm with gcd(ℓ,m) = 1, ℓO_K = (P₁⋯P_g)^e with distinct primes of degree d, where e = φ(ℓᵃ), d = ord_m(ℓ), g = φ(m)/d and edg = φ(f).
For reduced f ≥ 1 and a rational prime ℓ not dividing f, the automorphism ζ_f ↦ ζ_f^ℓ is the arithmetic Frobenius at every prime above ℓ.
For every odd prime p and every primitive p-th root used to define τ_p, τ_p² = (−1)^((p−1)/2)p.

concerns.concern: Opening prose assigns covolume 2^(−r₂)√|d_K| N(a) to 'nonzero fractional ideals'. The cited absolute-norm definition and owned covolume theorem define/prove this formula only for nonzero integral ideals; no fractional norm extension is supplied.

Remarks say 'the pieces S_k and their translates T_k all lie in the bounded set P, so every quantity involved is finite'. Only T_k lies in P; S_k lies in P+λ_k. Individual piece measures are finite, but vol(S) and the total series can be infinite. The proof handles extended sums correctly.
Fact F2 states, for 'nonzero real t', vol(tS)=tⁿ vol(S). The opened supplier states |t|ⁿ vol(S). Taking n=1, t=−1 and S=[0,1] refutes F2 as written; the proof itself uses positive t.

Remarks claim 'Both inequalities are equalities for the cube C=[−1,1]ⁿ and Λ=Zⁿ'. For n=2 the lower bound is 2, whereas (∏λ_i)vol(C)=4 and the upper bound is 4. The cube attains only the upper bound when n>1.

Remarks say class-group finiteness is proved 'later on this page, by combining this generation result with the finiteness of the set of integral ideals of bounded norm'. The finiteness theorem actually precedes this item and uses surjectivity from a finite set of representatives. Finite generation by small primes alone does not imply finiteness.

The displayed S-integer set quantifies over x∈K, but v_p(x) is defined immediately above only for x∈K×. No convention v_p(0)=+∞ or explicit adjoining of zero is supplied, so the claimed ring's definition is undefined at zero. ex-s-units-of-q step 2.3 nevertheless asserts that both rings contain zero.

Step 7.2 says 'p₀/q₀=2+√5' and 'p₁/q₁=9+4√5'. The opened convergent definition and this item's F7 give p₀/q₀=2/1 and p₁/q₁=9/4. The corresponding Pell elements are p₀+q₀√5 and p₁+q₁√5, not these rational quotients.

Step 1.1 sets c=log z and says the logarithms are defined although z∈(−2,−1); it needs log|z|, as used later. Step 7.1 additionally calls Q the covolume of the subgroup lattice in H. With the inherited Euclidean metric, that covolume is √3 Q; Q is the deleted-row determinant. The numerical value Q≈0.8492874506 checks correctly.
The last remark says the geometric inverse 'would agree only when ℓ≡1 mod f'. Equality instead holds whenever ℓ²≡1 mod f. For f=3 and ℓ=2, both maps send ζ₃ to ζ₃², although 2 is not 1 modulo 3.

The convention remark says the identity fails for ζ↦ζ^(b⁻¹) unless (b/p)=1. Its own F3 and step 3.1 prove (b⁻¹/p)=(b/p), so the same Gauss-sum action identity holds for every nonzero b, including nonresidues.

The first remark says inert degree four is 'the only case of the decomposition formula for K other than complete splitting', immediately listing possible orders {1,2,4}. Order two gives two degree-two primes: ℓ=19≡4 mod 5 is a concrete omitted case.

The Given fixes an arbitrary primitive fifth root. F2 qualifies τ₅=√5 by the standard complex root, but steps 2.1 and 3.1 use τ₅=√5 without imposing that choice. For ζ₅=e^(4πi/5), τ₅=−√5 and the intermediate equality −τ₅=−√5 is false. The stated Frobenius action on √5 remains correct independently of the choice.

The opening calls Q(√2) 'the quadratic subfield' of Q(ζ₈). There are three quadratic subfields: Q(i), Q(√2), and Q(√−2). The supplier correctly says 'a quadratic subfield' and explicitly avoids a uniqueness assertion.
